segments.text: The most famous thing about Judas Iscariot may be the least secure thing we think we know: why he did it.

segments.text: This episode asks a narrower question. Who was Judas according to the earliest surviving sources—and what can history responsibly recover before later explanation fills the gaps? His motive belongs to a separate episode.

segments.text: Start before the Gospels. Paul’s generally accepted letters are the earliest surviving Christian writings, but they never name Judas Iscariot. In First Corinthians, Paul says that Jesus took bread on the night he was “handed over.” The Greek verb can carry the sense of handing over or betrayal, but Paul does not identify who did it.

segments.text: The first surviving narrative portrait is Mark. Judas is introduced as “one of the Twelve.” He goes to the chief priests, who promise him money. Mark gives no amount and no explicit motive. Later, Judas arrives with an armed group and identifies Jesus with a kiss.

segments.text: That is the spare core of the earliest Gospel: an insider, a handover, promised money, and an arrest signal.
segments.tts_text: That is the spare core of the earliest Gospel: an insider, a handover, promised money, and an arrest signal.

segments.text: Matthew uses Mark but adds important details. Judas asks what he will be paid. The answer is thirty pieces of silver. After Jesus is condemned, Matthew says Judas regrets what he has done, returns the money, declares that he has betrayed innocent blood, and hangs himself. The priests then use the silver to buy a potter’s field.

segments.text: Luke also uses Mark, but his explanation is different. Satan enters Judas. The authorities agree to give him money, though Luke names no amount. In Acts, written by the same author, Judas acquires a field with the reward of his wrongdoing, falls headlong, and bursts open.

segments.text: Matthew and Acts therefore preserve materially different accounts of the field, the money, and Judas’s death. Readers have proposed harmonizations, but the texts themselves do not provide one.

segments.text: John’s portrait is later and more severe. John calls Judas a devil, says he kept the common purse and stole from it, and says Satan entered him after he received a piece of bread. In John’s arrest scene, Judas brings the force to the garden, but no identifying kiss is needed: Jesus steps forward and names himself.

segments.text: These are not four independent biographies. Matthew and Luke draw heavily on Mark. John is distinctive but later and strongly theological. When their details are compared, Judas becomes progressively more explained: money is numbered, remorse is narrated, Satan enters, theft becomes part of his character, and death becomes judgment.

segments.text: That development does not prove the later details are false. It means each addition must be tested rather than stacked as another independent witness.

segments.text: Even the name “Iscariot” is uncertain. “Man of Kerioth” is a familiar proposal, but scholars have offered many competing derivations. The surviving evidence does not establish his hometown, occupation, family, politics, or regional identity.

segments.text: A cautious historical reconstruction therefore keeps a very small core: Jesus chose a Jewish follower named Judas as one of the Twelve, and Judas later handed Jesus over—or enabled the authorities to arrest him. Beyond that, confidence drops quickly.

segments.text: We do not know Judas’s private motive. The sources offer money, satanic influence, scriptural fulfillment, and theological necessity. Modern reconstructions add political disappointment, attempted provocation, fear, or secret obedience. Those may be imaginable. They are not established history.

segments.text: The second-century Gospel of Judas does not solve the problem. It is a later Christian text, preserved in a much later Coptic manuscript, that gives Judas a special role in a different theological argument. Scholars still debate whether its Judas is privileged, condemned, or both. It is evidence for later Christian conflict—not Judas’s memoir.

segments.text: One further boundary is non-negotiable. Judas, Jesus, the Twelve, and the Judean leaders in these stories were Jewish. Rome carried out the execution. Judas cannot be turned into a symbol of Jewish greed, treachery, or collective guilt.

segments.text: What occurred: the strongest recoverable core is that Judas belonged to the Twelve and helped hand Jesus over for arrest.

segments.text: What survived: Mark’s spare account, Matthew’s silver and remorse, Luke–Acts’ satanic and death traditions, John’s darker characterization, and a later Gospel of Judas that rewrites the argument.

segments.text: What no one could know: Judas’s private motive, inner experience, or the exact chain of events behind every later detail.

segments.text: History can recover the act more easily than the man—and the man more easily than his motive.
